courses.name: Slow Blues Phrasing Workshop
courses.tagline: Shape vocal-like bends, vibrato, and space into expressive slow blues solos.

courses.name: Velvet Voicings: Chord Melody Mastery
courses.tagline: Weave lush extended chords and singing melodies into seamless solo neo-soul arrangements.

tree.summary: Neo-Soul Chord Melody in D: voicings, embellishments, chord melody, harmony, making music, built around the neo-soul & r&b vocabulary at your level.

exercises.name: Gmaj7 – F♯m7 – Em7 – Dmaj7 in drop-2 voicings
exercises.why: Drop-2 voicings voice-led through a progression are how jazz and neo-soul players comp with smooth inner voices.
exercises.instr: Hit each chord on beat 1 and the “&” of 2 (the Charleston rhythm). Each new chord is the closest inversion: watch which voices move and which stay.
exercises.watch: Big jumps between chords: pick the nearest inversion instead.
exercises.simplify: Whole notes, one chord per bar.

exercises.name: Gmaj7 – F♯m7 – Em7 – Dmaj7 in drop-2 voicings
exercises.why: Drop-2 voicings voice-led through a progression are how jazz and neo-soul players comp with smooth inner voices.
exercises.instr: Hit each chord on beat 1 and the “&” of 2 (the Charleston rhythm). Each new chord is the closest inversion: watch which voices move and which stay.
exercises.watch: Big jumps between chords: pick the nearest inversion instead.
exercises.simplify: Whole notes, one chord per bar.

exercises.name: Hammer-on embellishments: Gmaj7 – F♯m7 – Em7 – Dmaj7
exercises.why: Neo-soul and R&B players decorate chords with hammer-ons from a step below: the chord sings like a melody.
exercises.instr: Strike the chord with the top note a whole step low, hammer up to the chord tone, then pick a short melody across the top of the shape.
exercises.watch: The hammered note dying out; hammer firmly from close to the fret.
exercises.simplify: Chord and hammer only, no melody.

exercises.name: Vibrato on target notes
exercises.why: Even, in-time vibrato makes long notes sing.
exercises.instr: Hold each note for two beats with vibrato in time: two pulses per beat. Wrist rotation, thumb hooked or light.
exercises.watch: Vibrato that drifts flat or speeds up.
exercises.simplify: One pulse per beat.

exercises.name: Chord-melody: harmonize the D major scale
exercises.why: Chord-melody puts the melody on top of the chord; this harmonized scale is the first step to arranging tunes.
exercises.instr: The top note of each voicing is the scale; the chord under it changes (I, V, I, IV…). Let the top note ring loudest.
exercises.watch: Melody note buried under the chord.
exercises.simplify: Play only the top two strings.

exercises.name: Interval shapes from D
exercises.why: Every interval has a fixed shape on the neck; knowing shape + sound is how you play what you hear.
exercises.instr: Root, then the interval: minor 3rd, major 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, minor 7th, major 7th, octave. Sing each interval before you play it.
exercises.watch: Playing the shapes without listening; name each one as it sounds.
exercises.simplify: Only the 3rds and the 5th.

exercises.name: Chords of D major (7th chords)
exercises.why: Every key has seven chords built from its scale; knowing them by number (I, ii, V…) is how players talk and think about songs.
exercises.instr: Play up the key: Imaj7 – ii7 – iii7 – IVmaj7 – V7 – vi7 – viiø7, saying each numeral and its quality out loud. The voicings stay in one area of the neck.
exercises.watch: Mixing up which chords are minor.
exercises.simplify: Only I, IV and V.

exercises.name: Find the key by ear
exercises.why: Hearing the home note of a progression is the first step to playing along with anything.
exercises.instr: Don’t look at the chord names. Over the loop, hum the note that feels like “home”, find it on the low E string, then check it against the first chord.
exercises.watch: Guessing from the first chord instead of listening for the resolution.
exercises.simplify: Play single notes on one string until one sounds like home.

exercises.name: Echo phrases by ear
exercises.why: Copying short phrases in time is the fastest way to play what you hear.
exercises.instr: Hum a 2-bar phrase over the loop, then find it on the neck in the next 2 bars, inside the D major pentatonic. Start with 3-note phrases.
exercises.watch: Stopping the loop to search; keep it going.
exercises.simplify: 2-note phrases: the root plus one note.

exercises.name: Guide-tone line: Gmaj7 – F♯m7 – Em7 – Dmaj7
exercises.why: The 3rds and 7ths are what define each chord; connecting them smoothly is the skeleton of every good solo over changes.
exercises.instr: Play the 3rd then the 7th of each chord (or 7th then 3rd), always moving to the nearest one. Then improvise around this line over the backing.
exercises.watch: Big leaps between guide tones.
exercises.simplify: Only the 3rd of each chord, on beat 1.

exercises.name: Solo over Gmaj7 – F♯m7 – Em7 – Dmaj7: land on chord tones
exercises.why: Landing on a chord tone at each change makes a solo follow the harmony.
exercises.instr: Improvise with the D major pentatonic. On beat 1 of each new chord, land on its root or 3rd; use space between phrases and repeat ideas before changing them.
exercises.watch: Running the scale up and down without phrasing.
exercises.simplify: Whole notes: only the target notes, in time.

courses.name: Shred Foundations: Brown Sound Workshop
courses.tagline: Build tapping, tremolo picking, and dive-bomb control with fiery, rhythmic precision.

tree.summary: Shred Foundations in A minor: alternate picking, legato, arpeggios, harmony, making music, built around the metal vocabulary at your level.

exercises.name: 16th-note bursts on two strings (A)
exercises.why: Short, fast cells across a string change build the synchronized hands that shred lines need.
exercises.instr: Strict alternate picking, tiny motions. Play the cell 4 times, rest a beat, repeat. Speed comes from relaxation, not force.
exercises.watch: Tension creeping into the forearm as the tempo rises.
exercises.simplify: The same cell in 8ths.

exercises.name: A natural minor (aeolian), position 1 in groups of 3
exercises.why: Natural minor (Aeolian) is core vocabulary for this style; position 1 links to the shapes around it.
exercises.instr: Play in groups of 3 in 16ths, strict alternate picking. Say the root (A) each time you pass it; the root dots are what tie this shape to the chords.
exercises.watch: Speeding up on the easy strings and slowing on string changes.
exercises.simplify: Play it in 8ths at the same tempo.

exercises.name: Legato 3-notes-per-string: A harmonic minor
exercises.why: Pick once per string and let the fretting hand do the rest: the fluid sound of rock and fusion lead.
exercises.instr: Pick only the first note on each string. Hammer-ons going up, pull-offs coming down, every note the same volume.
exercises.watch: Weak hammer-ons and notes that fade.
exercises.simplify: One string at a time, then two.

exercises.name: Vibrato on target notes
exercises.why: Even, in-time vibrato makes long notes sing.
exercises.instr: Hold each note for two beats with vibrato in time: two pulses per beat. Wrist rotation, thumb hooked or light.
exercises.watch: Vibrato that drifts flat or speeds up.
exercises.simplify: One pulse per beat.

exercises.name: 3-string Am sweep arpeggio
exercises.why: Sweeps play a chord one note at a time with one continuous pick motion: shred and neoclassical vocabulary.
exercises.instr: One push through the strings going up, one pull coming down; lift each finger as soon as its note has sounded so notes don’t ring together.
exercises.watch: Notes bleeding into a strum.
exercises.simplify: Pick each note separately, slowly.

exercises.name: Tapping triplets in A
exercises.why: Tapping adds a third finger to the fretboard: wide, fast lines that picking can’t reach.
exercises.instr: Tap fret 17 with the picking hand (T), pull off to 10, hammer 15. Mute the other strings with both hands.
exercises.watch: The pull-off from the tap being quieter than the hammered note.
exercises.simplify: Tap and pull-off only, quarter notes.

exercises.name: A harmonic minor, position 1
exercises.why: Harmonic minor is core vocabulary for this style; position 1 links to the shapes around it.
exercises.instr: Play up and down in 16ths, strict alternate picking. Say the root (A) each time you pass it; the root dots are what tie this shape to the chords.
exercises.watch: Speeding up on the easy strings and slowing on string changes.
exercises.simplify: Play it in 8ths at the same tempo.

exercises.name: A Natural minor vs Harmonic minor
exercises.why: Natural minor and Harmonic minor share a root but differ by one or two notes; hearing that difference is what modes are about.
exercises.instr: Play Natural minor, then Harmonic minor, from the same root. Find the note(s) that change and lean on them: that's the color of each mode.
exercises.watch: Treating them as the same shape: they are not.
exercises.simplify: Play only strings 4–1 of each.

skills.title: Solo with speed and melody
skills.summary: Fast runs that land on chord tones.

exercises.name: Solo over Am – F – G – Am: land on chord tones
exercises.why: Landing on a chord tone at each change makes a solo follow the harmony.
exercises.instr: Improvise with the A natural minor (aeolian). On beat 1 of each new chord, land on its root or 3rd; use space between phrases and repeat ideas before changing them.
exercises.watch: Running the scale up and down without phrasing.
exercises.simplify: Whole notes: only the target notes, in time.

courses.name: Thumb Independence Mastery
courses.tagline: Command steady bass lines while melodies and inner voices move freely above.

tree.summary: Independent Thumb in E minor: thumb, thumb + melody, arpeggios, harmony, making music, built around the fingerstyle & classical vocabulary at your level.

exercises.name: Travis picking: E – C♯m – A – B
exercises.why: An alternating thumb bass under finger-picked melody notes: the core of folk and fingerstyle accompaniment.
exercises.instr: Thumb plays the bass on every beat, alternating between the root string and the next one up. Fingers fill the off-beats. Keep the thumb steady even when a finger misses.
exercises.watch: The thumb copying the fingers’ rhythm.
exercises.simplify: Thumb only for one bar, then add one finger.

exercises.name: Sextuplet bursts on two strings (E)
exercises.why: Short, fast cells across a string change build the synchronized hands that shred lines need.
exercises.instr: Strict alternate picking, tiny motions. Play the cell 4 times, rest a beat, repeat. Speed comes from relaxation, not force.
exercises.watch: Tension creeping into the forearm as the tempo rises.
exercises.simplify: The same cell in 8ths.

exercises.name: Thumb bass with percussive slaps
exercises.why: Modern fingerstyle turns the guitar into a band: thumb bass, a slap “snare” on 2 and 4, melody on top.
exercises.instr: Thumb on the low root. On beats 2 and 4, slap the strings with the side of the thumb/palm (the x hits): a muted, snare-like crack. Melody note on the “&” of 3.
exercises.watch: The bass note dying when you slap; keep the thumb steady.
exercises.simplify: Bass and slap only.

exercises.name: p-i-m-a arpeggios: Em – Am – B – Em
exercises.why: Classical right-hand independence: thumb on the bass, i-m-a on strings 3-2-1, every note even.
exercises.instr: p (thumb) bass, then i, m, a, m, i. Plant the fingers on their strings before each chord; rest strokes for a full tone.
exercises.watch: Uneven volume between fingers (a is usually weakest).
exercises.simplify: p-i-m only.

exercises.name: Chords of E minor
exercises.why: Every key has seven chords built from its scale; knowing them by number (I, ii, V…) is how players talk and think about songs.
exercises.instr: Play up the key: i – ii° – iii – iv – v – vi – vii, saying each numeral and its quality out loud. The voicings stay in one area of the neck.
exercises.watch: Mixing up which chords are minor.
exercises.simplify: Only I, IV and V.

exercises.name: Interval shapes from E
exercises.why: Every interval has a fixed shape on the neck; knowing shape + sound is how you play what you hear.
exercises.instr: Root, then the interval: minor 3rd, major 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, minor 7th, major 7th, octave. Sing each interval before you play it.
exercises.watch: Playing the shapes without listening; name each one as it sounds.
exercises.simplify: Only the 3rds and the 5th.

exercises.name: Chord-melody: harmonize the E major scale
exercises.why: Chord-melody puts the melody on top of the chord; this harmonized scale is the first step to arranging tunes.
exercises.instr: The top note of each voicing is the scale; the chord under it changes (I, V, I, IV…). Let the top note ring loudest.
exercises.watch: Melody note buried under the chord.
exercises.simplify: Play only the top two strings.

exercises.name: Gap click: keep the time yourself
exercises.why: When the click disappears for two bars, only your internal clock keeps you in time.
exercises.instr: Play the progression in steady 8ths. The click plays 2 bars and goes silent for 2: you should land exactly with it when it comes back.
exercises.watch: Rushing in the silent bars.
exercises.simplify: Quarter-note strums.
